## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Patrol officers and deputies who write incident reports from body-cam footage.
   [LYC] "Intros to Police, Sheriff, Transit, or University PDs that wrestle with video or paperwork overload."
   [LYC] "We auto-generate reports, verify narratives, and surface evidence instantly — cutting desk time by 60% and
   putting officers where communities need them most." → `roles[officer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.
   Author's choice: "at small and mid-sized police departments" stands for [LYC]'s "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers)".

2. **What (the job).** Get every call written up as a report, accurately, without the officer stuck at the desk.
   [LYC] "40% of a typical shift vanishes to transcribing body-cam footage, filling forms, and locating clips across
   siloed systems." [YCW] "Officers spend up to a third of their shifts manually transcribing body camera footage".
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** After a call, when the footage has to become a report; at the desk, often past end of shift.
   [PR] (Chief Sever) "an officer might not be as detailed if they're 'down 10 reports'". [PR] "End-of-shift reports,
   which provide an overview of incidents over an entire shift, will continue to be written exclusively by humans."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: incident report`. Author's choice: the window {7, DAYS} (spec 120: "every shift"
   reads as 7 DAYS) and Frequency 3 to 5 days out of 7 (an officer works about four or five shifts in seven; the posts
   say "a typical shift", so every shift worked). Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "a typical shift".

4. **Which people.** US police, sheriff, transit and university departments of 10 to 200 officers.
   [LYC] "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers) willing to co-shape features." [LYC] "We'll fly anywhere in North
   America to set you up within 48 hours—no strings attached." → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The department, per officer a month; the chief decides under a spending cap, the city council above it.
   [PR] "Sever said he's only able to authorize expenditures up to a certain amount without Heber City Council approval.
   Purchasing Draft One for around $30,000 per year would require such permission. Buying Code Four at around $6,000 to
   $8,000 per year would not." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: chief}`; Buyer and payer tests "Nobody else" (the
   chief alone), with "The city council" and "The city manager" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A side-by-side
   trial against Axon's tool", is from [PR] ("The Police Department recently completed free trial periods of two AI
   programs") and [CMP] ("We ran 30 days with Axon Draft One and 30 days with Code Four... 17/18 Officers chose Code Four
   at the end of the trial."); the other two items (a records-system check; the prosecutor's office agreeing) are the
   author's, the second from [BDN] (the district attorney: "It's not something that my office, or our PDs, have agreed
   is ready for use."). Commitment's step, "run a free pilot with a few officers": [LYC] "no strings attached"; [BDN]
   "he has provided a year of the software for free"; [PR] the free trial periods. Header: the outside payer (gap 2).

6. **Mechanism.** Footage in; a draft narrative in the department's format, each fact tied to its clip, with check
   words the officer must remove.
   [LYC] "Autofilled narrative reports that match your RMS schema and chain-of-custody rules." [LYC] "Real-time
   transcription & summarization — every body-cam or interview video becomes searchable text + key-frame timelined."
   [LYC] "One-click redaction — faces, plates, minors' voices, and PII are masked with CJIS-compliant logs."
   [BDN] (Cheng) "Essentially, we make it so that the patrol is reviewing the reports rather than writing the reports
   from scratch"; "Code Four inserts extraneous, random or incorrect information into the reports. If an officer doesn't
   remove that information, they cannot submit a final draft." [CMP] "Every report fact links to the source clip,
   transcript, and timestamp". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (footage uploaded before
   the shift ends — tested; typed into the records system; time to read a draft) and Adoption friction (read and
   correct every draft — tested; delete the check words). Relative advantage's two benefits: [LYC] "cutting desk time
   by 60%" (shorter_time) and [CMP] "Code Four analyzes every frame of body camera footage, not just the audio"
   (less_worry); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $30 per officer a month; the cost is the officers' report time.
   [BI] "Cheng said Code Four works with 25 police departments and makes money via a subscription model, which starts
   at $30 per officer a month." [PR] "Code Four is significantly cheaper at $30 per officer per month. Sever estimated it
   would cost Heber City between $6,000 and $8,000 annually." → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $30 to $30 per officer
   (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, HOURS 40 to 60 of the incident reports per officer a month: author's arithmetic from [YCW] "up
   to a third of their shifts" and [LYC] "40% of a typical shift", on 8-to-10-hour shifts and about fifteen shifts a
   month (a third of 8 hours x 15 = 40; 40% of 10 hours x 15 = 60). The rate, $37 an hour, is [BLS] "The median annual
   wage for police and detectives was $77,310 in May 2025" ($37.17 an hour), the author's stand-in: no source gives an
   officer's hour. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [PR] (a Heber City sergeant, of a report drafted with an AI tool) "This report would have taken me an hour, and it
   took me eight minutes." [CMP] (a chief, vendor-curated) "Code Four helped one of my guys who was 3 weeks behind
   reports finish his reports" (the quote goes on; its last words are not reproduced here). [BDN] (a researcher) "There's
   a lot of error there because of background noise: being on the side of a highway, of trucks driving by".

## Status today

Widened, same core. [SITE] today sells four products (report writing, investigations over phone dumps and jail calls,
redaction, a mobile field-capture app) and claims "Live in 200+ departments"; [YCP] reads "Modernizing the police
workflow." Customer counts in the press: 25 departments ([BI] 2025-11-19), about 50 ([BDN] 2026-02-24). Price today:
no public price list ([SITE], read 2026-10-22); the latest dated figure is [BDN] "If the department decides to continue
using it, they will pay $50 per officer per month, or about $3,000 to $5,000 a year for the small department." (after a
free first year).

## Could not be sourced

- **A launch-era price.** Neither [LYC] nor the site's archived snapshot of 2025-07-01 carries one; the earliest dated
  price is [BI]'s $30 per officer a month, six months after launch. It is used as the founder's price because it is the
  nearest dated figure and the price the company named publicly first; a reader holding the entry to the launch era
  should treat the price as one step later than the rest.
- **An officer's hour.** No source gives one; [BLS]'s median for police and detectives stands in.
- **The hours per officer a month.** The founders give shares of a shift, not hours; the 40 to 60 is the author's
  arithmetic (item 7).
- **A buyer title for the cap.** Only Heber City's chief is on record ([PR]); that every chief has a cap, and that the
  council and city manager are the other roles, is the author's reading.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person officer accounts.** None exists; officer occasions are scripted from [PR], [BDN]
  and [CMP] (the last vendor-curated).
- The footage-upload condition (tested Compatibility), the three Purchase friction items but the trial, and every pick
  are the author's.

screens.why1: As the chief who would buy this, being shown what the tool is before being asked about the buying decision is the obvious place to start.
screens.why2: Body-cam, narrative report, records format and redaction are everyday words in my shop, but 'check words they must catch' isn't anything we say and I'd have to reread it to guess it means planted errors the officer has to spot.
screens.why3: I know exactly how long my officers spend turning footage into reports and what our redaction workload is, so I can weigh this from my own department.

screens.why5: Calling Code Four 'a drafted narrative report' makes the product sound like the report itself rather than a tool that drafts it, and the belief says 'you' review and sign when it's my officers who sign, not me.
screens.why6: It says as a short card, but 'a drafted narrative report' as a name tag and 'check words they must catch' are clauses I'd stumble over hearing them once.

Your officers upload a call's footage, and it writes the narrative in your department's own records format, with every fact linked to the clip it came from and a few planted errors the officer has to catch before signing. It also redacts footage in one click and searches across it. The people building it believe your officers would review and sign instead of writing from scratch.
